title: Gotta Want It, Gotta Do It: The Motivational and Executional Hurdles to Student Success
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart reorganizes the character strengths posted in his ninth grade classroom into two hurdles that stand between students and success. The first is motivational, the Gotta Want It hurdle, where grit's passion, purpose, optimism, growth mindset, curiosity, and gratitude each give students a different reason to try. The second is executional, the Gotta Do It hurdle, covered by grit's persistence, self-control, social and emotional intelligence, and zest. He is motivated by a gap he still sees: despite the strengths on the wall, students stall on homework completion and change dramatically from room to room. His point is that motivation does not automatically become work, so teachers must diagnose which hurdle a given student is failing at. The post is a conceptual sorting, with the practical interventions promised for later.
points: Student ownership matters: a teacher can support but cannot be the savior who refuses to let a student fail.
Different students are driven by different motivators, as shown by his examples of students propelled by gratitude, passion, or optimism.
Motivation without execution is insufficient, as shown by students who respond to goal-setting and inspiring stories but do not turn that into results.
Sorting the strengths into motivational and executional groups gives a diagnostic lens for deciding what intervention a stalled student needs.
quotes: Before a kid can realize his or her potential in my ninth grade classes, he or she has to want to succeed. In David Conley’s words, there has to be a level of ownership within the student — none of this “I, the teacher, am not going to allow you to fail” stuff. I’m their teacher, not their savior.

Yet the strengths can be hard to hold together in a coherent fashion, and I think that limits the students and me from using them to solve the problems that daily face us. Because, even with the strengths on the wall and embedded in my instruction, the Snowball Kids still happen. The homework completion rates still stagnate.
But motivation isn’t enough. Many of my students are motivated when we do a goal-setting exercise or I give a Do Hard Things story, and yet too few translate that motivation into success.

You can be the most motivated person in the world, but that motivation must translate into doing the work if it’s going to take you anywhere. I’m pretty good at encouraging my kids to think and dream about who and what they want to be; I’m not as good at helping them actually do the work to gain the skills and dispositions their dreams will require.

How much easier would your work in the classroom be if kids fully developed these four Executional Strengths? When we design simple experiments and interventions to help kids develop these strengths, we’re working toward, truly, working smarter rather than harder.
